questions.learning_objective: Avoid assuming all pediatric myocarditis is caused by a routine viral infection.
questions.stem: Which statement about the cause of myocarditis in children is most accurate?

options.text: Viral illness is common, but infectious, immune-mediated, systemic inflammatory, drug-associated, and other causes must be considered in context
All pediatric myocarditis is caused by direct viral infection of cardiomyocytes
Immune-mediated myocarditis does not occur in children
A temporal relationship to a new medication makes myocarditis impossible
Myocarditis cannot be diagnosed unless a specific pathogen is identified

questions.rationale: Viruses are common triggers, but pediatric myocarditis has diverse infectious and noninfectious etiologies. Etiology matters because selected immune-mediated, drug-related, or specific infectious forms may alter treatment.

option_explanations.broad_causes: Correct. The etiologic differential should follow exposure history, systemic disease, laboratory clues, imaging, and selected tissue testing.
option_explanations.all_viral: Viral triggers are common but do not account for all cases, and direct myocardial viral infection is not proven by a preceding viral syndrome alone.
option_explanations.no_immune: Autoimmune and other immune-mediated mechanisms are recognized and can be clinically important when disease-specific immunomodulation is considered.
option_explanations.drug_excludes: New medications can be relevant exposures rather than exclusions, particularly when hypersensitivity/eosinophilia or an immune-mediated adverse effect is plausible.
option_explanations.pathogen_required: Many clinically valid myocarditis cases have no identified pathogen. Diagnostic confidence derives from the integrated cardiac syndrome, not mandatory pathogen discovery.

questions.board_pearl: 'Postviral' is a context, not an etiologic proof; always ask whether the cause would change treatment.

evidence.claim: Pediatric myocarditis has diverse infectious and noninfectious etiologies despite viral causes being common.
The 2025 ESC framework distinguishes multiple specific myocarditis etiologies with different treatment implications.

questions.learning_objective: Maintain a myocarditis diagnosis when no pathogen is identified if clinical/imaging evidence remains convincing.
questions.stem: A 6-year-old has a clinically and CMR-supported diagnosis of myocarditis, but an appropriate infectious evaluation does not identify a pathogen. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: The myocarditis diagnosis can remain valid; failure to identify a pathogen does not exclude myocardial inflammation
Myocarditis is excluded because a pathogen is required
Negative pathogen testing proves an autoimmune cause
The child must instead have congenital heart disease
Etiologic uncertainty means cardiac follow-up has no value

questions.rationale: Clinical myocarditis often lacks a proven infectious cause. Negative pathogen testing neither invalidates the cardiac diagnosis nor proves a specific noninfectious mechanism.

option_explanations.diagnosis_valid: Correct. Diagnostic and etiologic certainty are separate questions.
option_explanations.exclude: Modern myocarditis diagnosis can be clinical/CMR-supported or biopsy-proven without identifying a pathogen.
option_explanations.prove_autoimmune: Negative infectious testing broadens the differential but does not establish autoimmunity. Autoimmune attribution needs disease-specific evidence.
option_explanations.congenital: Congenital structural disease should be excluded when appropriate, but negative pathogen testing does not point automatically to it.
option_explanations.stop_followup: Follow-up is determined by the myocardial syndrome and residual risk, not whether the inciting cause was identified.

questions.board_pearl: Do not confuse 'cause unknown' with 'diagnosis unproven'.

evidence.claim: Pediatric myocarditis can be clinically/CMR diagnosed without identification of a causative pathogen.

questions.learning_objective: Describe IVIG as commonly used but not a universally proven regimen for idiopathic pediatric acute myocarditis.
questions.stem: An 8-year-old has acute non-COVID myocarditis with LV dysfunction but is now hemodynamically stable. The team asks whether IVIG should be presented to the family as proven mandatory therapy for every child with this diagnosis. Which statement is most defensible?

options.text: IVIG is commonly used and newer observational/meta-analytic data suggest possible benefit, but the evidence remains insufficient to present it as a universally proven mandatory regimen
IVIG is established by definitive pediatric randomized trials as mandatory for every case
IVIG has been proven harmful and should never be used in pediatric myocarditis
IVIG and corticosteroids have definitively equivalent benefit in all pediatric myocarditis subtypes
If IVIG is used, heart-failure and rhythm management are no longer necessary

questions.rationale: IVIG use is common in pediatric myocarditis and contemporary observational/meta-analytic studies report favorable associations, but randomized pediatric evidence remains limited and treatment practice varies. It should not be represented as a universally proven regimen.

option_explanations.ivig_uncertain: Correct. This framing acknowledges both current signals of potential benefit and the limitations of the evidence base.
option_explanations.ivig_mandatory: There is no definitive pediatric randomized evidence establishing mandatory IVIG for every phenotype and etiology. Some centers use it routinely; others individualize.
option_explanations.ivig_never: Existing evidence does not support a blanket prohibition. The issue is uncertainty of comparative benefit, not proven universal harm.
option_explanations.steroids_equiv: Steroid effects differ by subtype and evidence is heterogeneous. Some specific immune-mediated histologies have stronger rationale for immunosuppression than idiopathic cases.
option_explanations.replaces_support: Immunomodulation never substitutes for management of heart failure, shock, or arrhythmia. Physiologic support remains foundational.

questions.board_pearl: When evidence is observational and heterogeneous, the board-safe answer is often to state the uncertainty rather than invent a universal regimen.

evidence.claim: The AHA pediatric myocarditis statement notes common use of IVIG despite limited evidence supporting routine efficacy.
A 2026 pediatric network meta-analysis found signals of benefit for IVIG but called for high-quality randomized trials.
A 2026 PHIS observational analysis found associations between IVIG-containing strategies and lower mortality but cannot establish causality.

questions.learning_objective: Reserve a strong steroid recommendation for defined immune-mediated/histologic indications rather than assume routine benefit in undifferentiated myocarditis.
questions.stem: Which pediatric myocarditis scenario provides the strongest rationale for corticosteroid/immunosuppressive therapy rather than routine empiric steroid use for an undifferentiated case?

options.text: A defined immune-mediated or biopsy-directed inflammatory subtype in which immunosuppression is part of disease-specific management
Every child with troponin elevation after a viral illness
An asymptomatic child with normal cardiac testing and no evidence of myocarditis
Uncomplicated bacterial sepsis with no evidence of immune-mediated myocarditis
An athlete who has recovered and only wants faster sports clearance

questions.rationale: Routine corticosteroid efficacy in undifferentiated pediatric myocarditis remains uncertain, whereas selected immune-mediated or specific histologic subtypes can have clear disease-specific immunosuppressive strategies.

option_explanations.immune_histology: Correct. This is where identifying the mechanism or tissue subtype can materially change therapy.
option_explanations.every_case: Troponin elevation after a viral illness does not define a steroid-responsive mechanism. Empiric immunosuppression for every child would ignore etiologic uncertainty.
option_explanations.normal_heart: Without evidence of myocarditis there is no disease target for immunosuppression.
option_explanations.bacterial_sepsis: Steroids may have separate critical-care indications in some shock states, but bacterial sepsis without myocarditis is not a rationale for myocarditis-directed immunosuppression.
option_explanations.sports: Immunosuppression should not be used simply to accelerate return to sports; clearance depends on true clinical recovery.

questions.board_pearl: Immunosuppression is strongest when the mechanism is defined—not when the diagnosis is merely 'postviral myocarditis'.

evidence.claim: Routine immunotherapy evidence in pediatric myocarditis is limited, while specific immune-mediated/histologic forms may warrant immunosuppression.
Current ESC guidance provides etiology-specific immunosuppressive strategies for selected myocarditis subtypes.

questions.learning_objective: Recognize drug exposure plus eosinophilia/systemic hypersensitivity as a clue to eosinophilic myocarditis that may make EMB and disease-specific therapy important.
questions.stem: A 15-year-old develops chest pain, ventricular dysfunction, eosinophilia, fever, and a diffuse rash shortly after starting a new medication. He deteriorates with ventricular arrhythmia and shock. Which etiologic concern should be prioritized?

options.text: Drug-associated eosinophilic/hypersensitivity myocarditis, with urgent specialist evaluation and consideration of EMB because subtype-directed treatment may matter
Assume routine viral myocarditis and ignore the medication exposure and eosinophilia
Simple cutaneous drug allergy that cannot involve the heart
Physiologic athletic remodeling
Costochondritis with incidental ventricular dysfunction

questions.rationale: A new drug exposure, eosinophilia, systemic hypersensitivity features, and severe myocardial disease raise concern for eosinophilic myocarditis. In high-risk disease, tissue diagnosis may identify a subtype for which immunosuppression and withdrawal of the trigger have treatment implications.

option_explanations.eosinophilic: Correct. This pattern is precisely why exposure history, differential count, and selective EMB can be care-changing in myocarditis.
option_explanations.routine_viral: Viral myocarditis remains possible, but ignoring strong drug/hypersensitivity clues would miss an etiologic pathway with different treatment implications.
option_explanations.isolated_allergy: Drug hypersensitivity can be systemic and may involve the myocardium; severe ventricular dysfunction and arrhythmia cannot be explained as a skin-only reaction.
option_explanations.athletic: Physiologic remodeling does not cause acute rash, eosinophilia, shock, and ventricular arrhythmia.
option_explanations.costochondritis: Chest-wall inflammation cannot explain objective ventricular dysfunction or systemic hypersensitivity findings.

questions.board_pearl: In myocarditis, eosinophilia plus a new drug is not background noise—it may identify a treatment-relevant subtype.

evidence.claim: Eosinophilic and drug-associated myocarditis are specific etiologic forms for which histology and mechanism can direct treatment.
High-risk myocarditis with a potentially treatment-relevant subtype is a setting where EMB can be important.

questions.learning_objective: Recognize myocarditis as possible cardiac involvement of a systemic inflammatory/autoimmune disorder rather than force a viral label.
questions.stem: A 10-year-old with a known systemic autoimmune disease develops chest pain, elevated troponin, ventricular ectopy, and new LV dysfunction during a multisystem inflammatory flare. Which etiologic interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: Consider myocarditis as cardiac involvement of the underlying immune-mediated disease and coordinate disease-specific evaluation with cardiology/rheumatology
Assume the myocarditis is viral because viral disease is the only pediatric cause
A preexisting autoimmune diagnosis excludes myocarditis
Ignore the cardiac abnormalities because systemic inflammation can raise troponin without consequence
Use exercise testing during the flare to determine whether symptoms are inflammatory

questions.rationale: Systemic immune-mediated diseases can involve the myocardium and pericardium. The underlying disease may change both etiologic evaluation and treatment, so the autoimmune context should be integrated rather than ignored.

option_explanations.autoimmune_myocarditis: Correct. The multisystem flare and objective myocardial injury make immune-mediated cardiac involvement a meaningful working diagnosis.
option_explanations.must_viral: Viral causes are common but not exclusive, and the known systemic inflammatory disease is directly relevant to mechanism.
option_explanations.autoimmune_excludes: Autoimmune disease can increase, not eliminate, the possibility of myocarditis.
option_explanations.troponin_ignore: Troponin can be nonspecific, but ventricular ectopy and new LV dysfunction show clinically significant cardiac involvement requiring evaluation.
option_explanations.exercise: Exercise is inappropriate during active inflammatory myocardial disease and cannot safely distinguish etiologies.

questions.board_pearl: When myocarditis appears during a systemic inflammatory flare, ask whether the heart is another involved organ.

evidence.claim: Systemic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases can cause myocarditis/pericardial involvement and may require etiology-specific management.
Noninfectious etiologies are part of the pediatric myocarditis differential.

questions.learning_objective: Escalate evaluation for genetic/immune predisposition when clinically confirmed myocarditis recurs.
questions.stem: A 13-year-old has a second well-documented episode of myocarditis after complete apparent recovery from the first. Which additional consideration becomes more important than after a single isolated episode?

options.text: Evaluation for an underlying genetic cardiomyopathy or immune predisposition
Assume the same virus caused both episodes and no further etiologic evaluation is useful
Stop cardiology follow-up between episodes because function normalized previously
Immediate competitive-sports clearance because recovery occurred after the first episode
Routine tonsillectomy as standard prevention of recurrent myocarditis

questions.rationale: Recurrence changes the pretest probability of an underlying predisposition, including inherited cardiomyopathy genes or immune mechanisms. It should trigger specialist etiologic reassessment rather than repeated attribution to an unspecified virus.

option_explanations.genetic_immune: Correct. Recurrent inflammatory phenotypes can overlap genetic cardiomyopathy and merit a deeper pedigree/genetic and immune evaluation.
option_explanations.same_virus: Repeated viral triggers are possible, but assuming identical causation without investigation risks missing an inherited or immune substrate.
option_explanations.no_followup: Normalization of EF after one episode does not eliminate recurrence or residual electrical/tissue risk.
option_explanations.sports_now: Recurrent myocarditis increases the need for careful recovery assessment, not automatic clearance.
option_explanations.tonsils: Tonsillectomy is not a standard myocarditis-prevention strategy without a separate ENT indication.

questions.board_pearl: Recurrence is a diagnostic clue: look for the substrate, not just the next trigger.

evidence.claim: Genetic predisposition is increasingly recognized in myocarditis and should be considered in recurrent/familial presentations.
The 2025 ESC framework includes genetic testing when indicated in myocarditis/inflammatory cardiomyopathy.

questions.learning_objective: Use a family history of cardiomyopathy/sudden death to broaden evaluation beyond an isolated viral explanation even after a first myocarditis episode.
questions.stem: A 16-year-old has a first episode of clinically confirmed myocarditis. His mother has dilated cardiomyopathy and an uncle died suddenly at age 35. Which next consideration is most appropriate after acute stabilization?

options.text: Obtain a detailed pedigree and consider cardiomyopathy-focused genetic counseling/testing with cardiology
Do no further etiologic evaluation because a preceding viral illness proves a sporadic viral cause
Ignore the family history because genetic cardiomyopathy and myocarditis never overlap
Wait for a second episode before documenting the family history
Assume relatives never require evaluation if the adolescent's EF normalizes

questions.rationale: A strong family history of cardiomyopathy and premature sudden death raises concern for genetic susceptibility or an inflammatory presentation superimposed on inherited cardiomyopathy. Pedigree and genetics can affect the patient and family.

option_explanations.genetic_counsel: Correct. Genetics does not replace the myocarditis diagnosis; it addresses why this patient may be susceptible and whether relatives are at risk.
option_explanations.viral_only: A viral prodrome is common and does not erase a malignant pedigree. It may be a trigger rather than the entire explanation.
option_explanations.family_irrelevant: Inflammatory and inherited cardiomyopathy phenotypes can overlap; this false separation would miss important risk information.
option_explanations.screen_only_if_recurrence: Recurrence is one trigger for deeper evaluation, but a strong family history is already sufficient reason to investigate the substrate.
option_explanations.no_relative_eval: Family implications depend on the genetic/clinical findings and should be addressed through cardiology/genetic counseling rather than assumed away after EF recovery.

questions.board_pearl: A viral prodrome does not cancel a malignant pedigree.

evidence.claim: Contemporary myocarditis guidance emphasizes genetic predisposition, family history, and genetic counseling/testing.
Genetic testing is incorporated into the 2025 ESC myocarditis diagnostic framework when indicated.

questions.learning_objective: Treat a proven actionable infection in parallel with cardiac supportive care rather than expect anti-infective therapy to replace management of heart failure or arrhythmia.
questions.stem: A 7-year-old with myocarditis is found to have a specific active infection for which disease-directed antimicrobial therapy is indicated. The child also has LV dysfunction and ventricular ectopy. Which principle is best?

options.text: Treat the identified infection while continuing appropriate management of ventricular dysfunction, rhythm risk, and perfusion
Stop cardiac monitoring because antimicrobial therapy makes arrhythmia risk disappear immediately
Ignore an actionable infection because all myocarditis treatment is purely supportive
Delay heart-failure treatment until the infection has been eradicated
Assume the antimicrobial will reverse severe pump failure immediately

questions.rationale: When an etiologic infection has a validated specific treatment, cause-directed therapy complements rather than replaces management of the cardiac phenotype. Shock, heart failure, and arrhythmias still require direct supportive treatment.

option_explanations.parallel_treatment: Correct. Etiology and physiology are treated in parallel.
option_explanations.infection_only: Even effective antimicrobial treatment does not immediately eliminate myocardial electrical instability or restore ventricular function.
option_explanations.support_only: Many myocarditis cases have no proven specific therapy, but an actionable identified infection should not be ignored when treatment is indicated for that infection.
option_explanations.delay_support: Cardiac deterioration can progress quickly; physiologic support must not wait for microbiologic response.
option_explanations.assume_cure: Etiology-directed therapy may prevent further injury or treat systemic infection, but established myocardial dysfunction can persist and requires ongoing cardiac management.

questions.board_pearl: Treat the cause when it is actionable, but never stop treating the physiology.

evidence.claim: Current myocarditis guidance distinguishes supportive therapy from etiology-directed treatment for selected specific causes.
Pediatric myocarditis management remains driven by heart failure, arrhythmia, and shock severity while etiology is evaluated.

questions.learning_objective: Understand why identifying a specific histologic subtype can be more care-changing than simply confirming nonspecific myocarditis.
questions.stem: A 12-year-old with rapidly progressive myocarditis undergoes EMB at an advanced center because of shock, ventricular arrhythmias, and conduction disease. Why can the tissue result be especially valuable in this setting?

options.text: It can identify a specific histologic/etiologic subtype for which immunosuppression or other disease-directed therapy differs from routine supportive management
It provides an exact numeric prognosis that makes clinical follow-up unnecessary
It is equivalent to a respiratory viral swab and adds no other information
All myocarditis histologies are treated identically, so subtype is irrelevant
A tissue diagnosis eliminates the need for MCS, rhythm treatment, or heart-failure support

questions.rationale: The main value of EMB in high-risk disease is not simply to add the word 'biopsy-proven.' Histology, immunohistochemistry, and molecular evaluation can identify specific forms such as eosinophilic or giant-cell myocarditis in which disease-directed therapy and prognosis differ.

option_explanations.subtype_changes: Correct. This is the clinically meaningful reason to accept the procedural burden of biopsy in selected high-risk cases.
option_explanations.severity_number: Biopsy informs diagnosis and sometimes prognosis, but it does not replace longitudinal clinical assessment or provide deterministic outcome prediction.
option_explanations.viral_swab: Tissue can reveal inflammatory cell type, necrosis, immunohistochemical patterns, and selected molecular findings that peripheral respiratory testing cannot provide.
option_explanations.all_same: Specific myocarditis histologies have different natural histories and treatment approaches; assuming all are identical undermines the purpose of tissue diagnosis.
option_explanations.replace_support: Disease-specific therapy works alongside, not instead of, management of shock, arrhythmia, and heart failure.

questions.board_pearl: In fulminant disease, the biopsy question is not merely 'Is there myocarditis?' but 'Is there a subtype I can treat differently?'.

evidence.claim: EMB can identify treatment-relevant histologic subtypes in high-risk myocarditis.
The 2025 ESC guideline gives subtype-specific myocarditis treatment pathways informed by histology/etiology.
Contemporary registry data support EMB's continued diagnostic role in pediatric myocarditis.
